title: Close Pair in Position and Value
statement:
You get an integer array nums and two limits, indexGap and valueGap.

Return true if there are two different positions i and j that are close in both senses at once: |i − j| ≤ indexGap and |nums[i] − nums[j]| ≤ valueGap. Otherwise return false.

examples.why: 9 (position 1) and 7 (position 3) are 2 positions apart and differ by 2.
5 and 6 are close in value, but 3 positions apart. Sorting the values alone would wrongly pair them.
-3 and -1 differ by exactly 2. Negative values must land in the right bucket too.

hints: Only the last indexGap values matter when you look at a new value. That is a sliding window.
Inside the window you need: is there any value within valueGap of x? Sorting the window works, but there is a trick that avoids sorting.

Cut the number line into buckets of width valueGap + 1. Two values in the same bucket are always close enough. A close pair can otherwise only sit in neighbouring buckets. Keep at most one value per bucket for the window.

explain.intuition:
Walk left to right and keep the last indexGap values in a window, like a debounce that only remembers recent events. For each new value x the question is: does the window hold anything within valueGap of x?

Buckets answer that in O(1). Use width w = valueGap + 1 and put x into bucket floor(x / w). Any two values in one bucket differ by at most valueGap, so a second value landing in an occupied bucket means you are done. That also means each bucket holds at most one value while you are still searching. A close value in another bucket can only be in the bucket directly left or right, so you check just those two and compare the actual difference.
steps: Set w = valueGap + 1 and an empty map from bucket id to value.
For each index i, compute b = floor(nums[i] / w) (a real floor, so negatives go down).
If bucket b is taken, return true. If bucket b − 1 or b + 1 holds a value within valueGap, return true.
Store nums[i] in bucket b. If i ≥ indexGap, delete the bucket of nums[i − indexGap], which is about to fall out of the window.
pitfalls: Using truncating division for the bucket. In JavaScript Math.trunc(-1 / 3) is 0, which puts -1 and 1 in the same bucket. Use Math.floor.
Using width valueGap instead of valueGap + 1. With valueGap = 0 that divides by zero.
Removing the old value after the checks but forgetting the off-by-one: the window for index i is [i − indexGap, i − 1], so nums[i − indexGap] must still be there while you check i.

solutions.title: Check every nearby pair
solutions.idea: For each position, compare it with the next indexGap positions.

solutions.title: Sliding window of buckets
solutions.idea: Buckets of width valueGap + 1 hold at most one value each. Check the value's own bucket and its two neighbours, then slide the window.

followups: Solve it with an ordered set of the window instead of buckets. What does each step cost, and when might you prefer it?
The values arrive as a live stream and indexGap is a time window in seconds. What changes?
